title: Zinc and Alcohol: Depletion, Hangovers, and Safe Dosing
excerpt: Can you take zinc and drink? How zinc powers the enzyme that breaks down alcohol, how drinking drains zinc, what the hangover research shows, and how much is safe.
metaDescription: Can you take zinc and drink? How zinc helps break down alcohol, how drinking depletes it, what the zinc-for-hangover research shows, and safe doses.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** it's generally fine to take a normal zinc supplement and have a few drinks, and the two don't interact in a dangerous way. The real relationship runs the other direction. Your body needs zinc to break down alcohol, and drinking, especially heavy drinking over time, drains zinc out of you. There is one interesting small study linking higher zinc in the diet to milder hangovers, but there is no good evidence that taking a zinc pill before a night out will stop a hangover. This guide covers what zinc does in alcohol metabolism, how alcohol lowers your zinc, what the hangover research actually shows, how much is safe, and when to talk to a doctor.

**The quick rules:** Take zinc with food, not on an empty stomach, because zinc on an empty stomach often causes nausea, and alcohol already irritates the stomach. Stay at or under the adult upper limit of 40 mg a day from all sources combined unless a doctor has told you otherwise. Don't take extra zinc "to drink more safely." If you drink most days, the fix that matters is drinking less and eating better, and a doctor can check whether you're actually low.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and official nutrient guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before taking zinc if** you drink heavily on a regular basis, have liver disease, kidney disease, or a digestive condition like Crohn's disease, take antibiotics, diuretics, or penicillamine, or plan to take more than 40 mg a day. **See a doctor promptly if** you notice ongoing loss of taste or smell, slow-healing wounds, frequent infections, numbness or tingling in your hands or feet, or yellow skin or eyes. In an emergency, call 911.

## How Zinc and Alcohol Interact: The Short Chemistry Lesson

Zinc is a trace mineral, which means you need only a small amount, but that small amount is involved in a huge number of jobs. It helps hundreds of enzymes do their work, supports your immune system, helps wounds heal, keeps your sense of taste and smell working, and is needed to make DNA and proteins.

One of those zinc-dependent enzymes sits right at the start of alcohol metabolism.

### Zinc is built into the enzyme that breaks down alcohol

When you drink, your liver breaks alcohol down in two main steps:

1. **Alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH)** turns alcohol (ethanol) into **acetaldehyde**, a toxic compound that's a big contributor to the flushed, nauseous, poisoned feeling of drinking too much.
2. **Aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH)** turns acetaldehyde into acetate, which is relatively harmless and gets broken down further into carbon dioxide and water.

ADH is what biochemists call a zinc metalloenzyme. That just means zinc atoms are part of its structure. In the classic liver form of the enzyme, each half of the enzyme holds zinc: one zinc atom sits in the spot where alcohol is actually converted, and another helps hold the enzyme's shape together. Without zinc, ADH can't do its job.

That fact is where a lot of online claims come from, so it's worth being precise about what it does and doesn't mean:

- **It does mean** zinc is genuinely essential to alcohol metabolism. A person who is seriously zinc deficient may, in theory, handle alcohol less smoothly.
- **It doesn't mean** that extra zinc on top of a normal diet speeds up alcohol breakdown. If you already have enough zinc, your ADH already has the zinc it needs. Adding more is a bit like putting extra spark plugs in the glovebox of a car that runs fine.
- **It doesn't mean** zinc helps the second step. ALDH, the enzyme that clears acetaldehyde, doesn't depend on zinc the same way. So zinc isn't a tool for the acetaldehyde buildup behind hangovers or the "Asian flush."

### Zinc also matters for the rest of your body's response to drinking

Zinc is involved in other systems that alcohol stresses:

- **The gut lining.** Zinc helps keep the tight junctions between gut cells sealed. Research in animals and in people with alcohol-associated liver disease suggests zinc deficiency may make it easier for heavy drinking to make the gut "leaky," letting bacterial by-products reach the liver and drive inflammation.
- **Antioxidant defense.** Zinc is part of an antioxidant enzyme called superoxide dismutase (the copper-zinc form) and supports proteins called metallothioneins that help mop up reactive molecules. Alcohol metabolism generates a lot of these reactive molecules.
- **Vitamin A.** Zinc is needed to move vitamin A around the body and to convert it into the form your eyes use. Heavy drinkers who are low in zinc can have problems with vitamin A as well, which is one reason night blindness shows up in some people with alcohol-associated liver disease.

## Does Alcohol Deplete Zinc?

Yes, and this is the most solid part of the whole zinc-and-alcohol story. Drinking lowers zinc in several ways at once:

- **You absorb less.** Alcohol irritates and damages the lining of the small intestine, which is where zinc is absorbed. Regular heavy drinking reduces how much zinc you take in from food.
- **You pee more of it out.** Alcohol increases the amount of zinc lost in urine. This effect has been documented in heavy drinkers for decades, and it happens even before any liver damage.
- **You often eat less of it.** Heavy drinking tends to replace food. Alcohol supplies calories but almost no minerals, so a lot of drinking can crowd out zinc-rich foods like meat, seafood, beans, and seeds.
- **A damaged liver handles zinc poorly.** In people with alcohol-associated liver disease, low blood zinc is very common, and lower levels tend to go along with more advanced disease.

The National Institutes of Health Office of Dietary Supplements lists people with alcohol use disorder as one of the groups at higher risk of zinc deficiency, noting that alcohol both reduces zinc absorption and increases zinc loss in urine.

### What about a social drinker?

This is where the scare stories go too far. If you have a few drinks on a weekend and eat a reasonably normal diet, there's no good evidence that you're meaningfully zinc deficient because of it. One big night will increase zinc loss in your urine for a while, but your body keeps zinc reserves in muscle and bone and will rebalance when you eat normally.

The people who should actually think about zinc are:

- People who drink heavily most days, or binge often
- People with liver disease of any kind
- People who eat very little meat or seafood, especially vegetarians and vegans who also drink regularly, since plant zinc is harder to absorb
- Older adults with poor appetite
- People with digestive conditions that affect absorption, or who have had weight-loss surgery

### Signs you might be low in zinc

Zinc deficiency is hard to spot because the signs are vague and overlap with plenty of other problems. Common ones include:

- Loss of appetite or a dulled or changed sense of taste and smell
- Getting sick often, or infections that drag on
- Cuts and sores that heal slowly
- Hair thinning or skin rashes, especially around the mouth
- Diarrhea
- Poor night vision

None of these prove you're low on zinc. Blood zinc tests are also imperfect, because blood levels can drop during an illness or inflammation even when your body's stores are fine. That's one reason it's better to ask a doctor than to guess and self-treat with high doses.

## Zinc for Hangover: What the Research Actually Shows

This is the question most people are really asking, so here's the straight version.

### The 2019 diet study

The study you'll see cited most often is a 2019 paper by Joris Verster and colleagues, published in the *Journal of Clinical Medicine*, which looked at diet, alcohol metabolism, and hangover severity. Researchers had a small group of young Dutch adults record what they ate and drank, along with their hangover symptoms after a night of drinking.

The headline finding: people who got more zinc from their diet, and also more nicotinic acid (a form of vitamin B3), tended to report less severe hangovers. The authors suggested that because zinc is part of ADH and vitamin B3 helps form NAD+, the helper molecule both alcohol enzymes use, better intake of these nutrients might support smoother alcohol metabolism.

That's an interesting result, and it fits the biology. But it has real limits:

- **It was small.** A small number of participants means the result could easily be a fluke.
- **It was observational.** People weren't given zinc. Researchers just compared what people already ate. People who eat more zinc-rich foods may differ in lots of other ways, such as eating more overall, eating more protein, or drinking with food.
- **Diet records are rough.** Food diaries rely on memory and estimates, and they're notoriously imprecise.
- **It tested dietary zinc, not pills.** Nothing in it shows that a zinc supplement taken before drinking makes the next morning any better.

So the fair summary is this: there's a plausible reason zinc might matter, and one small diet study pointing that way, but **there is no good evidence that taking zinc supplements reduces hangovers.** No well-designed trial has tested it.

### Why zinc probably isn't a hangover tool for most people

Even if the diet finding holds up, it most likely reflects people who were getting too little zinc doing better when they got enough. That's how most nutrients work. Filling a gap helps; going beyond enough usually doesn't. If your diet already includes some meat, seafood, dairy, beans, nuts, or fortified cereal, you probably already have the zinc your ADH needs.

Hangovers are also driven by much more than how fast ADH works. Dehydration, poor sleep, inflammation, low blood sugar, irritation of the stomach, the acetaldehyde step, and compounds in darker drinks all play a role. Zinc touches almost none of that. For a fuller rundown of what drives a hangover and what has the best evidence, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

### Zinc in hangover supplements

Zinc shows up in a lot of hangover and "recovery" products, usually alongside B vitamins, vitamin C, electrolytes, and plant extracts. That's reasonable as a minor ingredient. Just be aware that:

- The zinc in these products is unlikely to be what makes you feel better or worse.
- If you also take a multivitamin and a zinc-containing cold product, the totals can add up fast. Check the labels and keep a running count against the 40 mg daily limit.

Our [vitamins for hangover guide](/never-hungover/vitamins-for-hangover) looks at the other common ingredients in these formulas, and the [multivitamin and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/multivitamin-and-alcohol) covers whether a daily multi makes sense if you drink.

## Can You Take Zinc and Drink Alcohol?

For most healthy adults, yes. There's no known dangerous interaction between a normal dose of zinc and moderate drinking. A few practical points make it go more smoothly:

- **Take it with food.** Zinc on an empty stomach is a common cause of nausea, stomach cramps, and even vomiting. Alcohol irritates the stomach too. Stacking the two on an empty stomach is a good way to feel sick. Taking zinc with a meal largely avoids this.
- **There's no ideal "before or after drinking" time.** No research shows that timing zinc around a night out changes anything. If you take it daily, pick a consistent mealtime and stick with it. Taking it with dinner the evening you drink, or with breakfast the next morning, are both fine as long as you've eaten.
- **Don't double the dose to make up for drinking.** Extra zinc doesn't protect you from alcohol, and big single doses are the ones most likely to upset your stomach.
- **Separate it from certain medicines.** Zinc can bind to some antibiotics (more on this below), so the timing matters if you're on one.

### Zinc lozenges and alcohol

Zinc lozenges are popular for colds. Using them while you drink isn't dangerous, but a couple of things are worth knowing. Lozenges can add up to a lot of zinc in a day if you take one every few hours, so read the label for the total. And if you're sick enough to be taking cold remedies, alcohol tends to make recovery slower by disrupting sleep and adding to dehydration. Many cold and flu products also contain other ingredients, such as acetaminophen or sedating antihistamines, that genuinely don't mix well with alcohol. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains why acetaminophen is the one to watch most closely.

Avoid zinc **nasal** sprays and gels entirely. In 2009 the FDA warned consumers to stop using certain zinc-containing nasal cold products after reports that people lost their sense of smell, sometimes permanently.

## How Much Zinc Is Safe?

Here are the official numbers from the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements for adults. These are general figures, not personal advice.

| Group | Recommended daily amount | Upper limit (all sources) |
|---|---|---|
| Adult men | 11 mg | 40 mg |
| Adult women | 8 mg | 40 mg |
| Pregnant adults | 11 mg | 40 mg |
| Breastfeeding adults | 12 mg | 40 mg |

A few things to keep in mind:

- **The upper limit counts everything.** Food, multivitamins, zinc tablets, lozenges, and hangover products all add up.
- **Many single-ingredient zinc pills are 25 to 50 mg.** A 50 mg pill alone is above the upper limit. That's not instantly harmful, but taking it every day for months without a reason and without a doctor's guidance isn't a good idea.
- **Doctors sometimes prescribe more.** People with diagnosed deficiency, including some with alcohol-associated liver disease, may be given higher doses for a set period. That should happen under medical supervision, with monitoring.

### What happens if you take too much

Short-term, too much zinc commonly causes nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, stomach cramps, diarrhea, and headaches. These can be easy to blame on a hangover, which is another reason not to take a big dose the morning after.

Long-term, the bigger concern is **copper**. High zinc intake over weeks to months blocks copper absorption in your gut. Copper deficiency can cause anemia, low white blood cell counts, and nerve damage that shows up as numbness, tingling, or trouble with balance. This has been well documented in people taking large doses of zinc for long periods, including from overuse of zinc-containing denture creams. Heavy zinc intake can also lower HDL ("good") cholesterol and may weaken immune function, the opposite of what most people take it for.

## Zinc Forms: Which One to Choose

If you and your doctor decide zinc makes sense, the form matters less than the dose, but there are differences:

- **Zinc gluconate, citrate, and acetate** are common, inexpensive, and reasonably well absorbed. Gluconate and acetate are the forms used in most lozenges.
- **Zinc picolinate and zinc bisglycinate (chelated zinc)** are marketed as better absorbed. There's some evidence for slightly better absorption, but it's not dramatic, and they're usually more expensive. Some people find them gentler on the stomach.
- **Zinc oxide** is cheap and common in multivitamins but tends to be absorbed less well than the others.
- **Zinc sulfate** is an older form that works but more often causes stomach upset.

Labels can be confusing. Some list the total weight of the compound, and others list "elemental zinc," which is the amount of actual zinc. The elemental figure is the one that counts toward your daily limit.

## Getting Zinc From Food

For most people who drink socially, food is the simplest and safest way to make sure zinc isn't a weak link. Good sources include:

- **Oysters**, by far the richest source, with a single serving providing several times the daily amount
- **Beef, pork, lamb, and dark-meat poultry**
- **Crab, lobster, and other shellfish**
- **Pumpkin seeds, cashews, and hemp seeds**
- **Chickpeas, lentils, and other beans**
- **Dairy**, such as yogurt and cheese
- **Fortified breakfast cereals**
- **Eggs and oats**, in smaller amounts

Plant sources contain compounds called phytates that bind zinc and lower how much you absorb. Soaking, sprouting, or fermenting beans and grains (as in sourdough bread) reduces phytates. If you eat a mostly plant-based diet and drink regularly, it's worth paying a bit more attention to zinc.

There's also a practical drinking angle here: eating a real meal before you drink slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood, and a meal with meat, seafood, beans, or dairy happens to carry zinc along with it. That's a better plan than any pill.

## Medications and Conditions That Affect Zinc

Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before taking zinc if you use any of these:

- **Quinolone and tetracycline antibiotics** (such as ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, doxycycline, and minocycline). Zinc binds to these in the gut and can make both the antibiotic and the zinc less effective. Pharmacists usually advise spacing them several hours apart. Many antibiotics also have their own advice about alcohol, so check that separately.
- **Penicillamine**, used for Wilson's disease and some types of arthritis. Zinc can reduce how well it works.
- **Thiazide diuretics** (water pills such as hydrochlorothiazide). These increase zinc loss in urine, and long-term use can lower zinc levels.
- **Iron and calcium supplements** in high doses, which can compete with zinc for absorption if taken at the same time.

And because zinc and copper are tied together, anyone with a copper-related condition should only take zinc under medical guidance.

## Zinc and Liver Health

Low zinc is extremely common in people with alcohol-associated liver disease, and researchers have studied zinc supplements as one part of treatment. Some small trials and reviews suggest zinc may help with certain complications, including problems with brain function caused by liver failure, but the overall evidence is mixed and not strong enough for zinc to replace standard care. This is a medical situation. If you have been told you have liver disease, or you have symptoms like yellowing skin or eyes, swelling in your belly or legs, or confusion, zinc is not something to manage on your own. See a doctor.

For a healthy person who drinks socially, there's no good evidence that zinc supplements protect the liver from alcohol. The things that actually protect your liver are the obvious ones: fewer drinks, alcohol-free days, and a decent diet.

## When to See a Doctor

Most people reading about zinc and alcohol don't need medical care. But check with a doctor if:

- You drink heavily most days and wonder whether you're low in zinc or other nutrients. A doctor can test you and look at the bigger picture.
- You have ongoing loss of taste or smell, slow-healing cuts, frequent infections, or unexplained hair loss or rashes.
- You've been taking more than 40 mg of zinc a day for weeks and notice numbness, tingling, weakness, trouble balancing, or unusual tiredness, which can be signs of copper deficiency.
- You have yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pain under your right ribs, or swelling in your belly. These can be signs of liver trouble and need prompt attention.

If you notice shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or confusion when you go without alcohol for a day or two, say so plainly to a doctor. Those can be withdrawal signs, and stopping suddenly after heavy daily drinking can be dangerous without medical support.

## Where DHM Fits In

Zinc and DHM sometimes show up in the same conversations because both get linked to alcohol metabolism, but they work in very different ways. Zinc is a nutrient your ADH enzyme needs, and it matters mostly if you're short on it. DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism, the liver, and the brain's response to alcohol. Most of that research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's promising but not proven.

There's no known problem with taking a normal zinc dose and DHM together. If you want to try DHM, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you're also weighing other minerals, our [magnesium and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/magnesium-and-alcohol) covers another mineral that drinking depletes.

No supplement makes heavy drinking safe, and none replaces eating, hydrating, and pacing yourself.

## The Bottom Line

- Zinc is built into alcohol dehydrogenase, the enzyme that starts alcohol breakdown, so your body genuinely needs it to process alcohol.
- Alcohol lowers zinc by reducing absorption, increasing loss in urine, and crowding out food. This mostly matters for people who drink heavily on a regular basis, have liver disease, or eat a low-zinc diet.
- One small 2019 diet study linked higher zinc intake to milder hangovers, but there is no good evidence that zinc supplements prevent or reduce hangovers.
- Taking a normal dose of zinc and drinking moderately is generally fine. Take it with food, and keep your total under 40 mg a day unless a doctor advises otherwise.
- Too much zinc causes nausea in the short term and can cause copper deficiency over time.
- If you drink heavily most days, ask a doctor about testing your nutrient levels rather than guessing with high-dose pills.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you take zinc and drink alcohol?**

For most healthy adults, yes. There's no known dangerous interaction between a normal zinc dose and moderate drinking. Take zinc with food, because zinc on an empty stomach often causes nausea and alcohol already irritates the stomach. Keep your total zinc from all sources at or under 40 mg a day unless a doctor has told you otherwise, and talk to a doctor first if you drink heavily, have liver or kidney disease, or take antibiotics or diuretics.

**Does alcohol deplete zinc?**

Yes. Alcohol reduces how much zinc you absorb from food, increases how much zinc you lose in urine, and heavy drinking often replaces zinc-rich foods. Low zinc is very common in people with alcohol-associated liver disease and in people who drink heavily over long periods. For an occasional social drinker who eats a normal diet, there's no good evidence of meaningful deficiency.

**Does zinc help with hangovers?**

There is no good evidence that zinc supplements prevent or reduce hangovers. A small 2019 observational study found that people with higher dietary zinc intake reported less severe hangovers, which fits zinc's role in the enzyme that breaks down alcohol. But that study looked at food, not supplements, and it was too small and too loosely designed to prove cause and effect. If your diet already contains enough zinc, extra is unlikely to help.

**Should I take zinc before or after drinking?**

No research shows that timing zinc around a night out makes a difference. If you take zinc regularly, take it with a meal at a consistent time of day. Avoid taking it on an empty stomach the morning after drinking, since that combination is likely to make you feel sick. Don't take a larger dose because you plan to drink.

**Does zinc help your body break down alcohol?**

Zinc is part of alcohol dehydrogenase, the liver enzyme that turns alcohol into acetaldehyde, so your body needs zinc to break alcohol down. But if you already have enough zinc, there's no good evidence that taking more speeds up alcohol metabolism. Zinc also doesn't help the next step that clears acetaldehyde, so it isn't a fix for alcohol flushing or a way to sober up faster.

**How much zinc is too much?**

The adult upper limit set by US health authorities is 40 mg a day from all sources, including food, multivitamins, lozenges, and supplements. Going above that occasionally can cause nausea, vomiting, cramps, and diarrhea. Taking high doses for weeks or months can cause copper deficiency, which can lead to anemia and nerve problems such as numbness and trouble with balance. Higher doses should only be taken under a doctor's supervision.

**Can I take zinc lozenges while drinking?**

They're not dangerous with alcohol, but lozenges can add up to a lot of zinc if you take several a day, so count them toward the 40 mg limit. Be careful with other cold and flu medicines, which often contain acetaminophen or sedating antihistamines that don't mix well with alcohol. Avoid zinc nasal sprays and gels entirely, since the FDA has warned that some have been linked to loss of smell.

**Is zinc good for your liver if you drink?**

People with alcohol-associated liver disease are often low in zinc, and doctors sometimes prescribe it as part of their treatment, though the evidence for its benefits is mixed. For a healthy social drinker, there's no good evidence that zinc supplements protect the liver from alcohol. Drinking less, taking alcohol-free days, and eating well do far more. If you have signs of liver trouble, see a doctor.
